# Abstract

Bluebottles (_Physalia_) are commonly observed at the ocean surface and stranded on beaches worldwide, yet little is known about their seasonality or how it varies among the five species recently recognized within the genus. Here we use a combination of machine learning and participatory science to identify and describe patterns in the occurrence of _Physalia_ species around the world. We test for seasonal patterns in beaching events and investigate regions of species biogeographic overlap to determine whether species exhibit differential temporal peaks in occurrence. For one such region, the Southwest Pacific, we incorporate new open-ocean genomic sampling to connect patterns in strandings to pelagic distribution. With new beaching samples and iNaturalist observations from the South Atlantic, Indian, and Southeast Pacific Oceans, we expand the known range of _Physalia minuta_ (previously only found in the Southwest Pacific Ocean). Finally, to aid the future monitoring of _Physalia_ across the globe, we present novel morphological characterizations of colony organization and architecture, and clarify the type specimen status for three species (_Physalia physalis_, _Physalia utriculus_, and _Physalia megalista_). We combine these descriptions with thousands of research-grade labeled photos and 168 annotated mitochondrial genomes for molecular barcoding. Taken together, our results present a comprehensive community toolkit to identify _Physalia_, which will advance our understanding and monitoring of geographic and seasonal occurrence of _Physalia_ stranding events across our shared ocean. 

# Introduction

Open-ocean environments host more diversity and population structure than previously thought [@norris2000pelagic; @peijnenburg2013high; @bowen2016comparative; @johnson2022speciation; @church2025population; @ahuja2026siphonophore]. This challenges assumptions about a well-connected ocean and suggests instead that biological and physical processes play a dynamic role in maintaining boundaries between populations. The distribution and occurrence of populations have been framed in terms of biogeography, describing genetic distances across spatial gradients to test, among other things, the role of isolation by distance [@mills2007global; @casteleyn2010limits]. But spatial divisions can tell only one side of the story [@goetze2003cryptic; @unal2010basin; @goetze2011population]; temporal divisions, such as seasonal patterns, are also critical in shaping interactions among populations. Cyclic fluctuations in ocean currents, winds, temperatures, and productivity play a significant role in defining species ranges and potential points of contact [@gaylord2000temperature; @white2010ocean; @sunday2012thermal; @abedon2025surfacing]. These processes are particularly relevant to the ocean-surface community (neuston), which is directly exposed to both atmospheric and oceanic fluctuations[@hempel1972neuston; @helm2021mysterious; @hunter2023scratching]. This unique assemblage represents one of the most enigmatic and understudied ecosystems in the ocean, and one that is uniquely imperiled by pollutants and plastics that accumulate at the ocean surface [@helm2021mysterious]. Therefore, it is necessary to explore spatiotemporal dynamics in neustonic communities to understand the relationships among oceanographic processes and biodiversity.

Testing the role of spatiotemporal structuring of ocean communities requires high-resolution species occurrence data over time and space. For many organisms, such data can be difficult to gather, given the massive distances to be monitored and the remote nature of open-ocean environments. But for charismatic organisms, participatory or citizen science can provide us large sample sizes through crowd-sourced observations. This is true for _Physalia_ (Hydrozoa: Siphonophora), pelagic cnidarians that sail the ocean surface and regularly wash ashore. On the participatory science website iNaturalist, there are more than 20,000 photographs of _Physalia_ from dozens of countries and across all seasons. At least 96% were research grade at the time of download, meaning verified by two or more identifiers, and associated with exact time and place. Analyzing patterns in the seasonal occurrence of _Physalia_ globally presents an opportunity to unpack seasonal structure in biodiversity at the ocean surface. 

In our previous study of _Physalia_ diversity [@church2025population], we used population genomic data to show that there are at least five lineages in the global ocean. Each lineage has a unique oceanic range and identifiable morphology. We identified four as species, and the fifth has since been described as _Physalia mikazuki_ [@yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia]. We also found regionally localized subpopulations with unique genomic signatures, as well as evidence of long-distance migration between subpopulations. These species overlap in parts of their ranges, but it is unclear how species boundaries have been maintained. One open question is to what extent these species co-occur temporally, or if they have distinct seasonal distributions that might reflect distinct source regions, or differential movement driven by regional winds and ocean circulation. Answering these questions is essential as _Physalia_ represent a significant component of the neustonic ecosystem, serving as a key predator [@purcell1984predation; @damian2022characterizing; @nunes2025predation]. They also have potentially significant impacts on human health and tourism, given the severity of their sting when encountered in near-shore environments [@stein1989fatal; @labadie2012portuguese; @cavalcante2020health; @maharani2021first; @banon2025toxicity; @suebsuya2025marine; @hewitt2026blowin]. Understanding seasonal fluctuations in the occurrence of different species, therefore, has direct implications for how to predict and manage human-_Physalia_ interactions.

To determine the spatiotemporal distribution of _Physalia_, we used a combination of machine learning and participatory science to identify global species occurrence, range, and seasonality. We classified 3,599 images of _Physalia_ uploaded to the participatory science network iNaturalist, and used these as training data for two approaches: first, to fine-tune a machine learning model, and second, as a ground-truth dataset for a group of community labelers (iNaturalist community) to classify the remaining images. Based on the combined annotation of more than 20,000 images, we describe species distributions over space and time including regions of range overlap, and identify different seasonal dynamics driving species-specific peaks in stranding each year. We also describe patterns of seasonal gradients (e.g. for _P. physalis_ in the Northwestern Atlantic), and further show that similar seasonal patterns occur in other ocean basins (e.g., _P. megalista_ peak in Oct.-Dec. at 30'S in the Pacific, Indian, and Atlantic Oceans). We also present genomic and morphological identification resources to advance future efforts in the field. With mitochondrial genomic data from the Southwest Pacific _Physalia_ specimens, we show that species inhabit different open-ocean ranges. The new genomic data of _P. minuta_ from the South Atlantic extends its previously known narrow distribution. Finally, we present a morphological comparison of live and preserved specimens of the five _Physalia_ species, distinguish aspects of their colony-level organization, and designate a lectotype for _P. physalis_ and neotypes for _P. utriculus_ and _P. megalista_. The combination of thousands of labeled photographs, 168 publicly available mitochondrial genomes, and diagnostic morphological characters will facilitate future identification and allow for continued monitoring and research of this understudied neustonic system.

# Results

## Identifying _Physalia_ species in images

Our analysis of a dataset of global observations of _Physalia_, using a hybrid semi-supervised machine learning approach and community labeling approach, resulted in 16,453 of 20,734 images identified to species level (@fig-classification A). The model could not differentiate between iNaturalist observations of _P. utriculus_ and _P. mikazuki_, so we treated these observations as one group noted as _P. utriculus/mikazuki_. This approach first employed manual labeling of 2,706 images and iterative fine-tuning of a classification model to generate a training dataset of 3,599 images (1,096 _P. physalis_, 1,293 _P. utriculus/mikazuki_, 1,032 _P. megalista_, 178 _P. minuta_). These were used to tune a machine learning classification model and also provided as a ground-truth reference to community labelers on iNaturalist. The model resulted in 7,566 high-confidence classifications, and the community made 13,979 assignments, 5,022 of which were of the same images (@fig-classification B). This difference is likely due to iNaturalist's use of atlases for preliminary IDs (see Methods). From the final dataset, 2,084 images that represented outliers from the known range of the species were manually confirmed by the authors, resulting in 1,093 corrections (954 reassigned to a different species and 139 marked unidentifiable).

Comparing labeled images between the model and community labeling, we observed strong consistency, with 4,899 out of 5,022 joint observations being shared (97.6%; @fig-classification B). Model validation showed an accuracy >80% for all species even without filtering on confidence, as calculated using 15% of manually labeled images that were held out during training (@fig-classification C-D). Given the strong variation in image quality and composition, condition of beached specimens, and the complex morphology of these colonial animals, we estimate this may be near the maximum possible accuracy. Visualizations of model attention (representing the pixels most highly weighted in making an assignment) show that the model is largely focused on the float and colony zones (@fig-classification E-F).

## Seasonal dynamics in regions of range overlap

Our previous study describing species ranges had identified several regions of overlap among _Physalia_ species, raising questions about potential ecological overlap and mechanisms maintaining species barriers. To investigate the potential role of differential seasonal partitioning, we used the classified images to assess seasonal occurrences in four regions, presented by ocean basin (@fig-seasonality-pacific, @fig-seasonality-atlantic). Each figure pairs two regions, showing where observations are distributed (A, B) and when they occur during the year (C, D).

Our results show striking differences in seasonality and distribution across species. In the Southwest Pacific (@fig-seasonality-pacific B, D), _P. minuta_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ exhibit strong seasonal turnover in their observations. _Physalia minuta_ is virtually unobserved in Southern Hemisphere winter months (no observations in Jul.-Aug.-Sep.). We also find that in summer months (Jan.-Feb.-Mar.) _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ observations are frequent in Eastern Australia, but rare in New Zealand and Tasmania, and vice versa for _P. minuta_. _Physalia megalista_ is observed throughout the year, with peak occurrence in Sep. and Oct. Strong overlap of species in both space and time includes between _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ and _P. megalista_ in Eastern Australia in Oct.-Nov.-Dec., and _P. minuta_ and _P. megalista_ in New Zealand in the same months.

These patterns are consistent across ocean basins. In Southern Africa (@fig-seasonality-pacific A, C) _P. megalista_ again shows peak occurrence in Sep. and Oct., and is absent or rare in Jan.-Feb.-Mar. _Physalia utriculus/mikazuki_ and _P. minuta_ are absent or rare in Jul.-Aug.-Sep., consistent with observations from the Southwest Pacific. Seasonality is statistically significant for every species and region examined: in each case the observation dates depart from an even spread across the year (S1 Table). Seasonality is strongest in _P. minuta_, whose records in eastern Australia and New Zealand are three times as concentrated as those of _P. megalista_ in the same region. These trends are robust despite seasonal changes in iNaturalist user effort, as measured by records of abundant beach species (hermit crabs, echinoderms) as a proxy for observer effort. Seasonal patterns persisted or were especially clear when effort was taken into account- see, for example, observations of _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in Southern Africa (S1 Fig): an anomalous peak in counts in late April is seen for both _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ and other commonly observed beach species, corresponding to a period of local public holidays. _Physalia minuta_ had previously only been reported from New Zealand and Eastern Australia, but we recovered _P. minuta_ in the South Atlantic (see below). iNaturalist observations in Southern Africa analyzed here were manually validated. _Physalia minuta_ and _P. physalis_ may also overlap in their seasonal distributions in Southern Africa. Therefore, Oct-Nov-Dec may represent a period of four concurrent species in that region (@fig-seasonality-pacific A, C).

Unweighted and daily-weighted versions of C and D are shown in S2 Fig and S3 Fig.](../figures/seasonality_pacific.png){#fig-seasonality-pacific width=100%}

In contrast to consistent signals across the Southern Hemisphere, we observed distinct seasonal patterns for the same species in the Southern and Northern Hemispheres. _Physalia physalis_ in the Caribbean and northwestern Atlantic (@fig-seasonality-atlantic A, C) shows a strong decrease in occurrence in Jul.-Aug.-Sep., but at low latitudes 20-30° S (@fig-seasonality-atlantic B, D), the same decline in occurrence is seen earlier (Apr.-May.-Jun.). Here turnover in species is again apparent: in the Gulf of Mexico, _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ is likely present when _P. physalis_ is at its lowest occurrence in Jul.-Aug.-Sep. The distributions of _P. physalis_, _P. utriculus/mikazuki_, and _P. megalista_ may overlap in the western South Atlantic in Jul-Aug-Sep (@fig-seasonality-atlantic B, D).

## Seasonal patterns in _Physalia_ occurrence in space and time

To examine seasonality within a region, we visualized circular median day for observations across the grid for each species in the regions examined in the previous section (@fig-gradients). 

In Southern Africa, we visualized the seasonal patterns of _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ (@fig-gradients C, D). The species’ peak occurrences happen at different times of year: _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ overlap in space and time, but they have distinct annual peaks in occurrence that do not overlap. _Physalia megalista_ peaks in Southern Hemisphere spring (Aug-Sep-Oct), and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in the summer to fall (Nov to Apr). We also observe latitudinal differences in the distribution of _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ on the eastern coast, ranging from the north in Tanzania (July) to the southern coast of South Africa (Jan-Apr).
In the Caribbean and northwestern Atlantic (@fig-gradients A, B), we observed that _P. physalis_ is distributed from Gulf of Mexico northward to the eastern coast of North America, ranging from late winter/early spring (Jan-Apr) to late summer (Jun-Sep) consistent with the northward flowing Gulf Stream, as observed in a previous study [@abedon2025surfacing]. _Physalia utriculus/mikazuki_ is observed in the Gulf of Mexico in the Northern Hemisphere fall (late Aug, Sep), a pattern similar to the replacement of _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in South Africa.
We have also visualized occurrences of _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in the Southwest Pacific, as well as _P. physalis_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in the western South Atlantic (S4A-D Fig). _Physalia megalista_ follows a latitudinal gradient from north (Oct) to south (Jan) on the Eastern Australian coast in the Southwest Pacific (S4A Fig). The patterns observed for other species are complex, and more data is necessary to interpret their distributions with respect to regional circulation and wind patterns, as well as to biological processes.

Equivalent panels for the Southwest Pacific and the western South Atlantic are shown in S4 Fig.](../figures/seasonal_gradients.png){#fig-gradients}

## Open-ocean distributions in the southwestern Pacific

In addition to our analysis of beaching observations, we collected open-ocean _Physalia_ specimens from the Southwest Pacific over multiple years and performed whole-genome sequencing to confirm their identity. We combined these with sequenced specimens collected from beaches in the same region to investigate the pelagic nature of their seasonality, given that this region has three overlapping species with distinct spatiotemporal patterns of stranding. 

Both _P. minuta_ and _P. megalista_ were collected from the open ocean east of New Zealand, with _P. minuta_ consistently (over multiple years) recovered west of ~152° W, and _P. megalista_ observed further east (~144-152° W), with the exception of a single _P. megalista_ observation at 168.6° W in 2025. These observations indicate each species has distinct open-ocean distributions within and outside the South Pacific gyre (@fig-openocean). 

Open-ocean transects were sampled at the same time of the year (April), therefore giving insight into interannual signals, but cannot provide data on other time periods. Collections at other times of the year may inform us of how _Physalia_ distribution changes, and how they move with the currents through the seasons. 

![**Genomic sampling in the South Pacific shows distinct pelagic distributions**. Sampling over multiple years shows _P. minuta_ in open waters East of New Zealand. In both years (2024 and 2025), observations further East were exclusively of _P. megalista_ (~144-152° W). All open-ocean specimens were collected in April, in both sampling years. meg=_P. megalista_, min=_P. minuta_, utr=_P. utriculus_.](../figures/open_ocean_sampling.png){#fig-openocean}

## Revised distribution of _P. minuta_

Sampling in our previous global analysis [@church2025population] was limited in the South Atlantic. To help fill this gap, we collected live specimens from St Helena, observed their morphology, and genetically sequenced them. Our results showed that four out of five sequenced samples were _P. minuta_, and one was _P. megalista_ (S5 Fig). _Physalia minuta_ was previously only observed in the Southwestern Pacific and considered to be a species with a discrete regional range. Observing _P. minuta_ in the South Atlantic indicates its range is larger than previously understood.
Based on these results, we performed a detailed examination of potentially missed observations of _P. minuta_ out of the expected range on iNaturalist. We confirmed isolated stranding events in November 2019 in Chile (SE Pacific) and in February 2018 in Western Australia. In Southern Africa, the records are not isolated but suggest seasonality: 23 of 25 observations, recorded in seven different years between 2016 and 2025, fall between October and January, with single records in April and September and none from May to August. These are consistent with a large open ocean range of _P. minuta_ in the Southern Pacific, Indian, and Atlantic Oceans.

## Morphological characterization of species

In order to establish robust features for morphological identification of species, we collected, observed and photographed live (@fig-morphology A-I) and fixed (@fig-morphology J-U) specimens of four species, in combination with the recent description of _P. mikazuki_. We also describe the typical postures for each species that may reflect underlying differences in tissue-level anatomy. Based on these results, we present the shared characters and diagnoses of species, as well as newly proposed standard common names in English. To make our results more accessible for the community, we also composed a dichotomous key to the five species (S1 Text).

### Proposed English common names
_Physalia_ have many common names across languages [@pugh2019history], several of which refer to a specific kind of a Portuguese sailing ship, the man-o-war or caravala, used from the 15th to 18th century. In the Pacific, especially Australia, _Physalia_ are also referred to as bluebottles, evocative of their striking color, and of their 'message-in-a-bottle' floating behavior. The common name Portuguese man-o-war has proven problematic, however, as the reference to the Portuguese ship is easily confused with a comment about their biogeography. In reality, the only _Physalia_ species known from Portugal is _P. physalis_, which is likely also the species to which the common name man-o-war was originally attributed.
To rectify this situation, and to provide a standard set of English common names that can be used to refer to these species worldwide:

- for _Physalia_, we propose the common name "bluebottles"
- for _P. physalis_, we propose this species retains the name "Portuguese man-o-war"
- for _P. utriculus_, the most widespread species and most abundant in English-speaking parts of the Pacific, we propose the name "common bluebottle"
- for _P. minuta_, we propose the name "little bluebottle"
- for _P. megalista_, distributed around the southern tips of continents, we propose the name "southern bluebottle"
- For _P. mikazuki_, several names have already been proposed, including Japanese man-o-war, crescent helmet man-o-war, and crescent moon-o-war [@yongstar2026physalia]. This species is found outside of Japan (including Mexico, Pakistan, and elsewhere), and is also not the only or even most commonly collected _Physalia_ species in Japan. We concur with the recently suggested "crescent helmet", and use the name "crescent helmet bluebottle" for consistency with the names of the other Indo-Pacific species above.

### _Physalia_ (bluebottle) characteristics across species

(B) Clusters contain tripartite groups, arranged on branches, diagram modified from [@totton1960studies]. (C) Tripartite groups contain a gastrozooid, gonodendron, and a tentacle with an associated palpon, borne on the cluster base. Orientation keys give the body axes for each diagram; colonies are left-handed (L.H.) or right-handed (R.H.) according to which side of the float bears the main zone (see @fig-morphology). (D-H) Images of main zones from each species; all identifiable palpons are false-colored in orange to highlight position. Specimens YPM IZ 112279 (D), YPM IZ 111519 (E), YPM IZ 111243 (F), and YPM IZ 112655 (G); panel H is a republished image of _P. mikazuki_ [@yongstar2025physalia] and is not to scale. (I-M) Proposed cluster arrangements, one for each species in D-H respectively, showing only palpon attachment points to highlight differences in organization. The question mark in M indicates that the arrangement for _P. mikazuki_ is provisional, inferred from a single published image.](../figures/colony_organization.png){#fig-colony width=68%}

Munro et al. previously summarized morphological features of _Physalia_ colonies, including that they are composed of a float, posterior zone, and main colony zone (@fig-colony A), and that they can be either left- or right-handed, depending on the attachment point of the principal tentacle and palpon [@munro2019morphology]. While _Physalia_ colonies are often illustrated with the tentacles, tentacular palpons (not homologous to palpons in other siphonophores [@mapstone2014global]), and other zooids draped below the colony ventrally (as seen in the lateral view in @fig-morphology A-E), we observed another common posture in live specimens of four species (@fig-morphology F-I). In this posture, the posterior zone is flared opposite the main zone (e.g., to the left for right-handed colonies), and the main zone is pulled parallel to the surface of the water. In this arrangement it is apparent that large gonodendra are borne on the ventral side of clusters, such that they hang below the colony (e.g., @fig-morphology H), while palpons and tentacles are borne on the dorsal side, such that they insert nearest the surface (e.g., @fig-morphology I). When seen from above in this posture, the float may have a sinuous appearance, especially for specimens of _P. utriculus_ (S6A Fig).

Historically, one of the challenges to defining morphological differences across specimens was in discerning differences in maturity from differences across populations. This is particularly difficult when considering tentacle numbers. Here we present the following descriptive statements as a paradigm that allows us to address this challenge: [1] As described by Totton in 1960 [@totton1960studies], we consider all _Physalia_ colonies to consist of clusters (Totton's "cormidia", see Munro et al. 2019 for discussion of terminology [@munro2019morphology]), each made up of tripartite groups arranged on branches, following Totton's usage [@totton1960studies] (@fig-colony B). Each tripartite group consists of a palpon and associated tentacle, a gastrozooid, and a gonodendron (@fig-colony C). [2] While all tentacles are associated with a palpon [@totton1960studies], we observe that principal tentacles are associated with palpons that can be easily identified, while accessory tentacles may have reduced palpons. [3] We define an axis of tentacle maturity that ranges from accessory tentacles with tentilla spaced apart, appearing as beads on a string, to principal tentacles that have tightly packed tentilla and a coiled appearance.

Using this paradigm, we can define differences in the colony-level organization across species. First, by observing the position of palpons associated with principal tentacles, we identified clusters along the main zone of the colony (@fig-colony D-H). Based on the position of these clusters, we observed a primary difference between _P. physalis_ and other species is that in the former, clusters are on independent cluster bases (extensions of the outer float [@munro2019morphology; @trochanowska2025blackwater]). In _P. megalista_, _P. minuta_, and _P. utriculus_, clusters are typically borne primarily on one cluster base, though in _P. megalista_ this may be divided into two or more, with one larger than the other. _Physalia minuta_ differs from _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus_ in having multiple palpons and associated tentacles of a similar maturity on the cluster base. In contrast, _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus_ show a strong gradient of size extending anterior and posterior to the largest palpon. In typical _P. utriculus_ colonies, adjacent palpons and tentacles are much smaller than the central palpon and tentacle. In _P. mikazuki_, we observe a somewhat central arrangement with multiple clusters of different size, possibly following a gradient. However, this arrangement is hypothesized, as it is inferred from a single published photograph of a specimen [@yongstar2025physalia].

### _Physalia physalis_ (Linnaeus, 1758), Portuguese man-o-war (@fig-morphology A, F)

Large _P. physalis_ colonies can typically be distinguished from other species by their relatively large crest (dorsal septa and ridge, which can be raised to form a sail), running nearly the length of the float, that may be raised to a height as large as the float, and by the main zone of the colony that can have as many as seven clusters of zooids [@totton1960studies], each with a principal palpon and tentacle. In a typical floating posture, there is often no visible gap between the main and posterior zone of the colony (@fig-morphology F). Clusters are borne on separate cluster bases, distributed along the anterior-posterior axis of the body.

Small _P. physalis_ may share some characteristics associated with other species, in particular _P. utriculus_. These may reflect shared patterns of growth, for example, small _P. physalis_ colonies may also have a single principal tentacle. Across all species, the float and crest are muscular and can rapidly change shape through contraction, which may lead to postures that are similar to other species. For example, if the anterior end of the float is extended, _P. physalis_ may appear to have the anterior projection associated with _P. megalista_.

_Physalia physalis_ colonies vary in color from blue, to pink, purple, and green, but specimens from the South Atlantic and Caribbean Sea in particular achieve a bright pink coloration that is not known from other species of _Physalia_ (S7A-B Fig). Colonies from both the North and South Atlantic may have reddish gastrozooids, also unique to _P. physalis_ (S7 Fig A, D). Other colonies have dark blue, purple, or blue-green gastrozooids and palpons, while gonodendra are light purple. The apex of the crest is often pink, but may have no obvious coloration. The large float is typically shaded blue or pink, and is not glassy or strongly opalescent.

### _Physalia utriculus_, common bluebottle (@fig-morphology B, G)

In our previous publication, _P. utriculus_ comprised two well-supported sister lineages, labeled B1 and B2 in Church et al. (2025). The neotype presented here for _P. utriculus_ (YPM IZ 110777) is a member of the B1 lineage; B2 was recently described as a separate species, _P. mikazuki_ by Yongstar et al. (2025) [@yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia].

The most reliable positive indicator of the lineage of _P. utriculus_ and _P. mikazuki_ is bright yellow coloration on the distal tip of gastrozooids (@fig-morphology B inset). Other than the distal tip, gastrozooids are typically a bright blue, as are palpons and principal tentacles, while gonodendra are light purple (S6B Fig). Crest coloration varies from pink to blue to purple or no color (S6 Fig). The anterior apex of the float may be colored green, yellow, or blue (S6 Fig A, C, D). Excluding the crest and anterior apex, coloration on the float is usually absent, and observation of a glassy transparent float is usually indicative of _P. utriculus_ (though very recently washed up specimens of all species have glassy, globular floats). The float of _P. utriculus_ may appear curved or S-shaped when viewed dorsally, though in live animals this can change quickly as the muscles in the float contract and relax.

_Physalia utriculus_ shares a strong central organization of the main zone with _P. megalista_. All zooids appear to be borne on a single cluster base, in contrast to _P. physalis_ that has multiple cluster bases. Small specimens of _P. utriculus_ may also resemble _P. minuta_ due to glassiness of the float and size, but they do not share the central organization of the main zone. 

#### _Physalia mikazuki_, crescent helmet bluebottle (@fig-morphology E, N)

The description by Yongstar et al. of _Physalia mikazuki_ [@yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia] specimens (B2 lineage) indicates many shared morphological features with _P. utriculus_ specimens (B1 lineage), such as the distinct bright yellow coloration of the gastrozooid distal tip, bright blue gastrozooids, light purple gonodendra, and variable crest and body coloration with a glassy float (S6 Fig, S8 Fig). The most prominent characteristic differentiating _P. utriculus_ from _P. mikazuki_ is the number of principal tentacles. _Physalia utriculus_ are most often associated with the presence of a single principal tentacle, while _P. mikazuki_ specimens have multiple. Genetic data have confirmed that rare _P. utriculus_ specimens have >1 tentacle (S9 Fig), and it has been suggested since at least 1910 that tentacle number can vary across colonies of _P. utriculus_ [@kawamura1910bozunira; @pugh2019history]. Therefore, the tentacle number alone should be treated with caution as a diagnostic character. Here we suggest that a more robust feature that appears to be distinct is the colony arrangement of zooids. In _P. mikazuki_, the main zone of the colony of the specimen shown in the original description has multiple clusters of zooids borne from distinct cluster bases (@fig-colony H, M). This is consistent with what we observed in the larger of the two fixed specimens that have been sequenced for genomic analysis (@fig-morphology U).

Furthermore, one trait noted as distinct for _P. mikazuki_ in the Yongstar description is the number of zooid clusters in the main and posterior zone. However, the number of clusters has not been counted in the _P. utriculus_ or other _Physalia_ spp. across growth forms or its range, and it is possible this character varies with natural growth, as is true of other features of _Physalia_ colonies [@totton1960studies]. Additionally, the Yongstar description noted a gastrozooid morphology that may be different between _P. mikazuki_ and _P. utriculus_ [@yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia], however, gastrozooids are highly elastic due to their function, and much of the variance depends on how they are contorted at the time of fixation or observation, making them unreliable for species diagnoses.

Here we report observations of specimens that match the described morphology of _P. mikazuki_: colonies with dense main zones bearing multiple principal tentacles and associated palpons, and yellow-tipped gastrozooids (S8 Fig). These specimens, observed alive off the southern coast of Indonesia, vary in size (from ~3 to ~10 cm total float length), suggesting this is not correlated with the overall size of the colony. We hypothesize that, if these features prove reliable for _P. mikazuki_ identification, the range of this lineage extends throughout the Pacific and Indian Oceans, consistent with preliminary indicators from barcode data (MK084614.1), and our previous work [@church2025population].

### _Physalia minuta_, little bluebottle (@fig-morphology C, H)

_Physalia minuta_ was described in detail in our previous manuscript [@church2025population], but here we add the following observations. The float of beached and fixed specimens often has an elongated cylindrical shape (@fig-morphology L, R). In contrast to _P. utriculus_, _P. minuta_ colonies commonly have multiple principal tentacles and associated palpons at apparently similar levels of maturity, but unlike both _P. utriculus_ and _P. mikazuki_, they do not have brightly yellow-tipped gastrozooids. Zooids are borne from a single cluster base, such that the main zone of the colony has a "bunched" appearance, as opposed to elongated along either the dorsal/ventral or anterior/posterior axis. The combined characters of multiple principal tentacles and palpons, large gonodendra (indicating a mature colony), and a small size is strongly indicative of _P. minuta_. 

Zooid and tentacle coloration varies from bright blue to dark blue-green; gastrozooids may have pale cream-colored distal tips (S10B Fig). The float is typically without color except for the anterior apex, which may be green (S10 Fig A, C). In live specimens, the crest may be raised (@fig-morphology C), but in beached or fixed specimens it is typically fully relaxed (@fig-morphology R).

### _Physalia megalista_, southern bluebottle (@fig-morphology D, I)

_Physalia megalista_ is best recognized by the shape of the float and crest. In typical specimens, the float is elongated, with a prominent projection of the float beyond the anterior point of insertion of the crest (i.e., the crest is "incomplete"). In a relaxed posture, this projection of the float may appear shorter (@fig-morphology D), but when disturbed, the muscles are contracted such that the anterior projection is raised perpendicular to the water (@fig-morphology I). It is common to find specimens of _P. megalista_ in this position on the beach. Another common posture has both the anterior and posterior apices of the flared on the opposite side of the main zone, giving the float a "horned" appearance (S11B Fig). The crest of _P. megalista_ is distinct in having a crimped appearance along the dorsal surface (@fig-morphology D).

_Physalia megalista_ may have one or multiple principal tentacles. These are generally borne from one cluster base, though in large specimens there may be adjacent smaller cluster bases (S11A Fig). Like _P. utriculus_, the tentacles and palpons of _P. megalista_ exhibit a strong central organization such that the most distal tentacle and palpon are the largest, and those adjacent to the anterior and posterior are progressively smaller. There is also often a prominent gap between the posterior and main zone, as in _P. utriculus_ (@fig-morphology I). Unlike most _Physalia_, however, the main zone of the colony typically has more tentacles and palpons at late stages of maturity (@fig-morphology I).

Zooid and tentacle coloration is typically a dark blue-green, with palpons more green than tentacles. In some specimens in the South Atlantic, accessory tentacles may have red coloration (S11C Fig). The float is often opalescent purple and blue-green, and rarely glassy. The crest often has a lavender apex with green at the bases of the septae (indentations at the base of the crest, see S11 Fig A, D). 

### Type material

Type material is designated here for three species. For the two species
described recently, the existing type material is listed for completeness; no
further designation is made for either.

#### _Physalia physalis_

_Holothuria physalis_ Linnaeus, 1758: 657 [@linnaeus1758systema], the original combination of _Physalia physalis_, was founded on a composite series. The protologue cites Rumphius (Rumph. mus. 49, Ambon), Sloane (Sloan. iam. 1: 7, t. 4, f. 5, Jamaica) [@sloane1725voyage], the _Chinensia Lagerströmiana_ (Chin. lagerstr. 40, f. 6), Browne (Brown. iam. 386, Jamaica) and Osbeck (Osb. iter. 284, t. 12, f. 1) — the _Chinensia Lagerströmiana_ and Osbeck accounts deriving from Swedish East India Company voyages between Gothenburg and Guangzhou, and the Rumphius record from the Indo-Pacific. Under Articles 72.4.1 and 72.5.6 of the ICZN Code, the specimens described and illustrated are syntypes.

These accounts likely do not describe a single species of _Physalia_. Sloane's figured animal, _Urtica marina soluta purpurea oblonga, cirris longissimis_, and Browne's _Arethusa crista subrubella venosa_ are both western Atlantic, and Sloane's illustration is consistent with _Physalia physalis_. The Osbeck and _Chinensia Lagerströmiana_ accounts derive from Indo-Pacific voyages and are less clearly assigned.

So far as is known, a single alcohol-preserved syntype survives: UPSZTY 112, in the Museum of Evolution, Zoology Section, Uppsala University, from the Magnus Lagerström donations of 1748 and 1750 [@wallin2001linnaean]. It bears Thunberg's _Mus. Lagerstr._ label, and was recently photographed by Dr P. Cárdenas (@fig-morphology J). Based on the shape of the float and of the main zone of the colony, with a dense curtain of colony bodies and tentacles, we refer it to _Physalia physalis_, in agreement with the diagnostic characters given above.

To clarify the taxonomic status of the nominal species, we hereby designate UPSZTY 112, deposited in the Museum of Evolution, Zoology Section, Uppsala University, as the lectotype of _Holothuria physalis_ Linnaeus, 1758, the type species of _Physalia_ Lamarck, 1801, currently _Physalia physalis_ (Linnaeus, 1758). The remaining syntypes, including all specimens figured or described in the works cited above, become paralectotypes. Linnaeus gave the habitat only as _in Pelago_, and no syntype carries locality data. The Lagerström material was collected on Swedish East India Company voyages between Gothenburg and Guangzhou, which ran south through the Atlantic, around the Cape of Good Hope, across the Indian Ocean and through the Sunda Strait into the South China Sea. The type locality of the lectotype can therefore be given no more precisely than open ocean somewhere along this route.

#### _Physalia utriculus_

No type material of _Physalia utriculus_ is known to survive. _Physalia utriculus_ (Gmelin, 1788) was illustrated by La Martinière (1787) [@lamartiniere1787insects] from a specimen observed at approximately 20°N, 179°E during the La Pérouse expedition; Gmelin (1788) [@linne1788systema] supplied the name. Under Article 72.5.6 of the ICZN Code the specimen figured constitutes the name-bearing type. That specimen cannot be extant: La Martinière died with the expedition in 1788 when both vessels were lost, and only drawings, journals and correspondence dispatched from Kamchatka and Botany Bay reached France. We have consulted the history of the expedition and find no indication that any preserved specimens survived the voyage.

To clarify the taxonomic status of the nominal species, we designate as neotype YPM IZ 110777, Yale Peabody Museum Invertebrate Zoology collection, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America, collected by C. Simon on 19 July 2023 at 21.400790 latitude, -157.734500 longitude, Kailua Beach, Oahu, Hawai'i. The specimen agrees with La Martinière's figure and description in the characters given above, and was taken in the central North Pacific at approximately the latitude of the original observation, as near the original type locality as is practicable. It is the property of the Yale Peabody Museum, which maintains a permanent research collection accessible for study.

#### _Physalia mikazuki_

Type material was designated in the original description [@yongstar2026physalia]: TUM 112960, Tohoku University Museum, Sendai, Japan.

#### _Physalia minuta_

Holotype: NIWA 173305, New Zealand National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (NIWA) Invertebrate Collection in Wellington, New Zealand. Designated in the original description [@church2025population].

#### _Physalia megalista_

No type material of _Physalia megalista_ is known to survive. Lesueur and Petit described and illustrated the species from animals observed during the Baudin expedition, and their account gives no indication that specimens were preserved [@peron1807voyage]. We enquired with the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris, whose invertebrate registers do not extend before 1865, and searched its databased collections together with the archival record of the expedition, including the professors' assembly minutes held at the Archives nationales. Fluid-preserved invertebrates from the voyage do survive at the MNHN, but no cnidarians appear among the databased material and no _Physalia_ has been located.

Neotype: Western Australian Museum (WAM) in Perth, Western Australia, Australia under catalog number WAM-Z88480. The specimen was collected by K. Tullis on 3rd of August 2018. -31.908144 latitude, 115.754811 longitude at the Peasholm Dog Beach, Scarborough, Western Australia, Australia. The species was named and illustrated as _P. megalista_ by Lesueur and Petit in 1807 [@peron1807voyage] based on animals observed in the Indian Ocean near Western Australia. In the Atlas volume [@peron1807voyage], the name _P. australis_ is used in the main text, but not to describe the species. For consistency with subsequent publications, we use _P. megalista_ [@pugh2019history; @church2025population].

# Discussion

As new _Physalia_ species are described from the open ocean [@church2025population; @yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia], it becomes critical to provide resources to facilitate their identification and monitoring. To accomplish this purpose, we have provided here an integrated dataset of thousands of classified photographs, detailed descriptions of morphology, curated reference panels of genes and mitochondrial genomes, and maps of the ranges and seasonality of _Physalia_ species. Together, this toolkit can be used by citizen scientists, naturalists, and researchers across the globe, including in undersampled regions, such as South and Southeast Asia, Eastern Africa, and parts of South America. Our hope is that morphological descriptions and spatiotemporal data will boost interest and accuracy of worldwide iNaturalist community efforts, and advance future efforts to understand the ranges, seasonality, and diversity of _Physalia_. 

Our results show that at least four _Physalia_ species (_P. physalis_, _P. utriculus/mikazuki_, _P. minuta_, _P. megalista_) have distinct seasonal patterns and cross-basin distributions. In each case, there are notable species-specific patterns as well as periods of significant overlap in space and time. For example, in the southwestern Pacific, we observe that _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ and _P. minuta_ share seasonal patterns of peak occurrence in the Southern Hemisphere summer months. Their distributions, however, are quite distinct, with _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ nearly absent from New Zealand beaches but occurs in Eastern Australia, while _P. minuta_ shows the reverse pattern. _Physalia megalista_, by contrast, is abundant in both locations and displays a distinct seasonal pattern of occurrence. This suggests that the dominant species found on a given beach cycles over time. Similar patterns of turnover are observed between _P. megalista_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in Southern Africa, and _P. physalis_ and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in the Gulf of Mexico. Our exploration of circular median day of observations shows a latitudinal shift throughout a year for some species (_P. megalista_ in Eastern Australia, _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ in Southern Africa, _P. physalis_ in North America). The observed patterns are likely a result of transport processes governed by ocean circulation (e.g., Eastern Australian Current, Agulhas Current, Gulf Stream) and winds. Understanding the relationship between observed patterns and these processes requires detailed regional surveys across species in the future.

Environmental processes that influence the distributions of _Physalia_ have been the subject of research, but their focus is largely on the processes that bring adults to shore where they can have significant economic and health implications [@headlam2020insights; @macias2021model; @fierro2021new; @bourg2022driving; @bourg2024ocean; @martins2024unravelling; @roca2025unravelling; @carvalho2026spatiotemporal; @hewitt2026blowin]. In adults, movement is mediated by interactions of seasonal wind patterns and surface ocean circulation. Handedness of _Physalia_ likely impacts the outcomes of beaching (as explained in [@totton1960studies; @munro2019morphology; @pugh2019history]). Due to challenges in reliably determining handedness from beached specimens, we have not investigated how this feature, which determines the direction a colony sails in response to wind, might influence seasonal trends in strandings. Handedness represents an important next area of study, to investigate how this asymmetry might direct dispersal within and across species at global and regional scales. Additionally, at juvenile stages _Physalia_ spend a part of their life cycle under the water surface [@totton1960studies]. Their reproductive structures detach from the floating animal, then sink to a depth where they spawn and fertilize [@richter1907entwicklung; @steche1907genitalanlagen; @totton1960studies; @oguchi2024physalia; @gonzalezrajal2026integrative]. _Physalia_ larvae spend an unknown amount of time in the water column in a pelagic phase until they inflate a float, which raises them to the ocean surface [@totton1960studies]. Depending on the depth at which the embryo forms, and how fast they emerge to the surface, their movement may be influenced by the subsurface oceanographic processes for a part of their life cycle. To understand how species follow distinct spatiotemporal trends, it will be critical to learn more about their reproductive biology, including finding gametes or larvae at depth to estimate dispersal. Additionally, it may be that seasonal occurrence is largely indicative of the presence of preferred prey (generally fish) of each species and life stage. More research on differences in prey specificity and gut contents will shed light on how distinct patterns of seasonality reflect specialization on distinct fish populations.

To advance future studies of different aspects of _Physalia_ biology, we also provide morphological descriptions of four species (_P. physalis_, _P. utriculus_, _P. minuta_, and _P. megalista_), and a discussion on recently described _P. mikazuki_ [@yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia]. Despite this, several key questions about the morphological differences in _Physalia_ remain unanswered, particularly around the complex lineages of yellow-mouthed species like _P. utriculus_ and _P. mikazuki_. Further studies of their reproduction, development, growth patterns, and variation across their ranges will be crucial in establishing how genetic variation tracks morphological variation in coloration, tentacle and zooid number, and overall colony architecture. In particular, we reiterate the caution of previous authors [@totton1960studies; @pugh2019history] that, because certain traits vary throughout growth and development, studying the morphology of different-sized specimens across species is essential to understand what fixed differences are between lineages. Without such data, we find it difficult to diagnose specimens of _P. utriculus_ from their sister lineages based on the number of tentacles, zooids, or shape of the gastrozooids alone. 

Further exploration of the range and seasonality in the broad _P. utriculus_ lineage in particular has great potential to advance efforts to understand their biology. _Physalia utriculus_ has the broadest range of all species, from Texas (USA) to the Pacific coast of Ecuador, and has corresponding patterns of regional diversity in genetic subpopulations [@church2025population]. Studying the processes that allow a lineage to remain cohesive across such vast geographic ranges has the potential to shed light on what drives dispersal and gene flow across ocean basins. At the same time, evidence that a sister lineage (_P. mikazuki_) with similar morphology maintains a distinct and identifiable genotype despite strong overlap in ranges suggests that barriers to gene flow can arise in open waters [@church2025population; @yongstar2025physalia]. Further research to distinguish the proximal causes of these barriers can shed light on the origins of the complex and fascinating neustonic community. 

# Materials and Methods 

## Participatory science images

iNaturalist.org was accessed for participatory science observations on several occasions across the lifetime of the project, using the site's observation export tool. An initial dataset of 20,007 images was downloaded on June 4, 2025 and used for training, retaining research-grade observations (`taxon_id=117305`, `has[]=photos`, `quality_grade=research`, `identifications=any`, `verifiable=true`, `spam=false`). A final dataset of 20,734 observations was downloaded on August 14, 2025 using the same query, except that observations of any quality grade were retained (`quality_grade=any`); all of these were classified, of which at least 19,989 (96.4%) were research grade at the time of download. In addition, datasets on other commonly observed beach species (hermit crabs, echinoderms) were downloaded on August 22, 2025 as a measure of observer effort (`taxon_id=47398` and `taxon_id=47548`, `quality_grade=any`, `identifications=any`, `verifiable=true`, `spam=false`). All datasets analyzed here are included at <https://github.com/shchurch/Physalia_spatiotemporal_patterns>. Images not associated with a precise location were excluded (30 images from the final _Physalia_ dataset); all remaining images carried a timestamp.

A subset of ~4,000 images was examined manually and preliminarily assigned to species based on the characters described in previous work [@church2025population]. These were preferentially selected to include key regions of species overlap (New Zealand, Brazil, etc.) as well as regions with only one previously known species (Eastern North America, Hawai'i), to create a balanced and rich training dataset containing images with _Physalia_ of different sizes, shot at different angles and at various stages of decomposition. From this subset, 2,706 images could reliably be identified to species and were selected as the initial training dataset.

## Image classification via semisupervised learning

The initial training dataset was used to fine-tune a pretrained model, google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k (a Vision Transformer, ViT), using Python with PyTorch and the HuggingFace Transformers library. Model tuning was performed for 15 epochs, after which the model was redeployed to classify the remaining images. High-confidence (>90%) images were examined for their distribution over geographic range, and images falling outside previously understood ranges for each species were manually examined. Labels were either accepted, reassigned, or images were marked as likely unidentifiable given current morphological understanding (for example, juvenile specimens with a globular float and few zooids (colony bodies) were deemed indistinguishable). Outlier regions for species were defined as follows: _P. physalis_, records occurring outside the Atlantic basin (Indian and Pacific Oceans, longitude > 30°E; northeastern Pacific, longitude < −100°W, latitude > 0°N; southeastern Pacific, longitude < −60°W, latitude < 0°S); _P. megalista_, records north of 15°S; _P. utriculus_, records in the North Atlantic (longitude −100° to 20°E, latitude 15°–70°N) and New Zealand region (latitude −49° to −33°S, longitude 165°–180°E); _P. minuta_, records north of 15°S or west of 110°E. Confirmed new labels were then added to the original training dataset, and this process was repeated, resulting in a final training dataset of 3,599 manually confirmed images and 995 records flagged as unidentifiable.

A final image classification model was fine-tuned on the final training set, using an ensemble of three google/vit-base-patch16-224-in21k models with temperature scaling calibration and focal loss (γ = 2.0), for 10 epochs, using a 70/15/15 split for training, testing, and validating the training data. Final model accuracy was evaluated using a confusion matrix (@fig-classification C-D); overall accuracy on the held-out set was 83.8%. This model was deployed on the remaining images, of which 7,566 were assigned labels above a confidence threshold of >65% and were incorporated into the spatiotemporal dataset. A relatively lower confidence was used here to maximize classifications included in downstream steps, including comparison with community labels and manual inspection of geographic outliers.

## Community labeling images

The final training dataset of 3,599 manually confirmed images was provided to the iNaturalist community, who initiated a project to relabel the remaining images from around the globe. Authors S.H.C. and C.W.D. assisted the community in this work, responding to specific questions and comments on iNaturalist as tagged. iNaturalist community members determined the best course of action for relabeling, opting to use atlases for initial identifications based on previously understood ranges, and evaluating images in areas with known overlap. By August 14, 2025, 13,979 images had been labeled to species, at which point labels were downloaded and incorporated into the spatiotemporal dataset.

Final labels for the spatiotemporal dataset were determined by combining the training, classified, and community-labeled datasets in sequence. Each source was taking precedence over those before it: manual training labels, an initial round of manual correction, model classifications above the confidence threshold, community identifications, and a final round of manual correction. Labels for images marked as unidentifiable during initial training were removed as potentially unreliable. Manual inspection of geographic outliers (n=2,260) was performed to confirm the identity of any images that would extend the known range of species. After finding genetic evidence that the range of _P. minuta_ extends to the South Atlantic (see below), authors S.H.C. and D.D. additionally re-examined manually corrected samples, as well as all observations from the South Atlantic Ocean and Indian Ocean.

Neither iNaturalist nor machine learning-defined labels could differentiate between _P. utriculus_ and _P. mikazuki_ [@yongstar2025physalia; @yongstar2026physalia], as there is currently not enough information on the differences in their morphology for high-confidence species identification (see discussion below). Therefore, we treated all _P. utriculus_ as indistinguishable from _P. mikazuki_, and labeled them as _P. utriculus/mikazuki_.

## Seasonal occurrence characterization

To visualize potential seasonal patterns, we combined classified observations across years and visualized occurrence in three ways: [1] spatially, across four three-month epochs of the year; [2] daily, counting observations within defined regions; and [3] calculating the circular median calendar day of observations across a grid to analyze spatiotemporal occurrence. To account for potential confounding effects of iNaturalist user effort, we normalized to observations of abundant and commonly reported beach species (hermit crabs and echinoderms). These were chosen because they are conspicuous, abundant on many of the same beaches, recorded by many of the same observers, and present in all regions examined and on every calendar day of the year. Normalization followed two approaches: a raw ratio of daily _Physalia_ observations to proxy beach species, and a model-based normalization. For the latter we fitted a generalized additive model to the daily counts of proxy species in each region, with a cyclic cubic regression spline on day of year (20 basis functions) and Poisson errors, so that the fitted effort curve joins smoothly across 31 December. Each _Physalia_ observation was then weighted by the inverse of the fitted effort on its day of year. Further, comparing differences in species occurrences in the same region provides an internal control for user effort, as iNaturalist observations were originally recorded agnostic to species. To measure how strongly seasonal each species is in each region, we calculated a seasonality index _R_ from the dates of all observations, the mean resultant length of the dates treated as angles: it runs from 0 when records are spread evenly across the calendar to 1 when they all fall on a single day. We tested whether each distribution differs from an even spread using a Rayleigh test. _R_ is inflated when few records are available, so we report beside it the null _R_, the value expected from an evenly spread set of the same size (S1 Table).

## Genetic and phylogenetic analyses

### Sample collection

In addition to iNaturalist data, to advance our understanding of _Physalia_ distributions, we also collected specimens for genetic analyses. Specimens were collected in the Southwest Pacific and South Atlantic. The Southwest Pacific collections happened during two cruises aboard the Sea Education Association’s SSV _Robert C Seamans_. The first cruise took place from March 26th to May 3rd, 2024, from Lyttelton, Aotearoa, New Zealand to Pepe’ete, Tahiti, French Polynesia. The second cruise took place from April 3rd to May 16th 2025 from Lyttelton, Aotearoa, New Zealand to Mo’orea, French Polynesia. _Physalia_ was collected twice a day with 335 µm mesh neuston tows at a speed of 2 knots for 0.5 hour at 10:30 am and 10:00 pm, weather permitting. Tentacle tissue was subsampled and preserved in a DNA shield at -20℃ (Zymo Research, Orange, CA, USA), while whole specimens were preserved in 100% ethanol. Additional beached specimens from this region were collected in Breaker Bay, Foxton Beach, Lyall Bay, and one specimen from Perth (Western Australian Museum loan) collected on the coast, Eastern Indian Ocean. The South Atlantic specimens were collected at Sandy Bay Beach, St Helena (British Overseas Territory, United Kingdom), during two periods: September 24th, 2025, and January 11th to 20th, 2026. Specimens were stored in 100% ethanol and, for some, in formalin for morphological purposes, and photographed. Information on sequenced specimens can be found in S2 Table (`Supp_Table_specimens.tsv`).

### DNA extractions and whole-genome sequencing

The samples (n=20) used for short-read Illumina whole-genome sequencing were stored in 100% ethanol or DNA Shield (Zymo Research, Orange, CA, USA) (see `Supp_Table_specimens.tsv`). The same procedure was used for all samples. A piece of a tentacle was used as input for all of the samples, except for one degraded sample from St Helena, where we used a piece of float (YPM IZ 116019). DNA was extracted using the E.Z.N.A.^®^ Mollusk & Insect DNA Kit following the manufacturer’s instructions, with an overnight digestion step at 60℃. Yale Center for Genome Analysis processed the genomic DNA and prepared libraries for Illumina NovaSeq paired-end 150bp whole-genome sequencing (WGS) (10x coverage).

The 28 specimens collected on the 2025 Southwest Pacific cruise were sequenced on the Oxford Nanopore platform (ONT sequencing). Tentacle samples in DNA Shield (Zymo Research, Orange, CA, USA) of these 28 specimens were extracted using the Qiagen DNEasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). If available, about 5 mg of tissue was minced and digested. Whole genomic DNA was quantified and qualified on a Nanodrop One (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). The samples were then sequenced on Oxford Nanopore minION Mk1C and Mk1B platforms using the 24-barcode rapid PCR sequencing kit (SQK-RPB-114.24) on the ONT flow cell version FLO-MIN114 R10.4.1. We used a factory protocol with recommended reagents (New England Biolabs LongAmp Hot Start Taq 2X Master Mix NEB M0533, Ipswich, MA). Each sample was sequenced on two flow cells.

All 48 new WGS libraries (28 ONT, 20 Illumina) were deposited in the NCBI SRA under BioProject PRJNA1509992. SRA and BioSample accession numbers for each specimen can be found in S2 Table (`Supp_Table_specimens.tsv`).

## Read quality control and mitochondrial genome assemblies

 For subsequent analyses, we used previously published _Physalia_ WGS libraries (n=151) [@ahuja2024giants; @church2025population], and added the new Southwest Pacific and South Atlantic samples (n=48). The raw reads were checked with a quality control pipeline, implemented using Snakemake [@molder2021sustainable] and available in this repository (see Data Availability) under `pipeline/`, with separate folders for ONT and Illumina.

For the Illumina libraries, we took the first 10 million read pairs from each library, trimmed them with Trimmomatic, run with standard parameters for Illumina adapters [@bolger2014trimmomatic], and ran them through FastQC, Kraken2 (standard contaminant database) [@wood2019improved] and sharkmer v1.0.1 [@dunn2026sharkmer] (metazoa, cnidaria, and bacteria PCR primers; `-n 100 -k 31`). The reads were also mapped with BWA [@li2013aligning] to a human genome [GRCh38, GCA_000001405.15], to check for human contamination. Mitochondrial genomes were assembled directly from the trimmed reads using GetOrganelle (custom seed of siphonophore genomes, -R 10, --reduce-reads-for-coverage inf, --max-reads inf) [@jin2020getorganelle] and annotated with MITOS2 v2.1.9 (--orih 0, --oril 0, --trna 0, --intron 0, --linear, -c 4) [@donath2019improved] and tRNAscan-SE v2.0.12 (-O, -g gcode.invmito) [@chan2021trnascan].

ONT libraries were basecalled in real time during the sequencing run by MinKNOW. MinKNOW also demultiplexed the samples and removed adapters, and filtered reads at its default mean quality threshold of Q8. We took the first one million reads from each library and ran them through FastQC and sharkmer with the same primer sets (`-n 100 -k 21`).

Mitochondrial genomes were assembled from the ONT libraries using a separate pipeline. Reads were first mapped to a reference set of siphonophore mitochondrial genomes with minimap2 (`-x map-ont`) [@li2018minimap2], the mapped reads subsampled with seqtk to a cap of one million reads that was not reached in practice, and assembled with Flye (`--nano-raw --genome-size 20k --meta`) [@kolmogorov2019assembly]. GetOrganelle was then run on the resulting assembly graph (`get_organelle_from_assembly.py -F animal_mt`), and the assemblies annotated with MITOS2 v2.1.9 [@donath2019improved] and tRNAscan-SE v2.0.12 [@chan2021trnascan] as above. Assemblies were recovered for all 28 samples. These were used for species identification (below) but, because their quality varied relative to the reference mitochondrial genomes, they were not deposited publicly; they are provided in the mitochondrial genome alignment in this repository (see Data Availability).

Of the 171 mitochondrial genomes assembled from the Illumina libraries, 168 are deposited in GenBank. Two were withheld, being the two longest recovered, each approximately 420 bp above the modal genome length of 15,037 bp and with annotation tables inconsistent with the remainder, and one specimen (YPM IZ 104465) already has a published mitochondrial genome (OQ957220.1).

### Phylogenetic analyses

Phylogenetic trees were built from four single markers: the mitochondrial _cytochrome oxidase I_ (_COI_) and _16S rRNA_ genes, and the nuclear _18S rRNA_ gene and the internal transcribed spacer region (_ITS1_, _5.8S rRNA_ and _ITS2_, with flanking partial _18S_); and separately from whole mitochondrial genomes.

For the two mitochondrial markers, sequences were taken from the MITOS2 [@donath2019improved] annotations of the assembled mitochondrial genomes, supplemented by sharkmer products for samples without an assembly. The two nuclear markers were recovered by sharkmer alone, for all samples in which sharkmer returned a product. Where a sample yielded more than one sequence for a marker, the longest was retained. One sample (SEA2025-Ph277) was excluded from the gene trees, as its assembly was of low quality and it yielded no sharkmer product at any marker.

Published _Physalia_ and _Rhizophysa_ sequences were retrieved from GenBank on 5 August 2026 for each marker, excluding whole-genome and transcriptome assemblies and this study's own submissions, yielding 25 sequences for 16S, 4 for 18S, 80 for _COI_ and 53 for ITS. _Rhizophysa_ sequences were used as outgroups where available: 13 for 16S, 2 for 18S and 10 for _COI_, the last including accessions GQ120038, GQ120039, GQ120040, GQ120041 and AY937377. No _Rhizophysa_ ITS sequence is available, so the ITS tree is unrooted and is presented midpoint-rooted. The full list of GenBank accession numbers used for each marker is available in the GitHub repository accompanying this manuscript (see Data availability).

Sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.525 [@katoh2013mafft] using `--adjustdirectionaccurately --auto`, and trees inferred with IQ-TREE 3.0.1 [@nguyen2015iq] using 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates [@hoang2018ufboot], with substitution models selected by ModelFinder under the Bayesian information criterion [@kalyaanamoorthy2017modelfinder]. The selected models were TN+F+I+R2 for 16S (199 tips), HKY+F for 18S (185 tips), TIM2+F+R3 for _COI_ (257 tips) and JC+R3 for ITS (239 tips).

Two mitochondrial genome trees were inferred. First, a tree of all 168 deposited _Physalia_ mitogenomes included with this manuscript, plus three _Rhizophysa_ outgroup mitogenomes, used to evaluate phylogenetic relationships between species; second, a tree with an additional 31 mitogenomes, including 1 previously deposited (YPM IZ 104465) and 30 deemed to be insufficient quality (assembly, completeness) for deposition, used to evaluate identity of sequenced specimens. Every species assignment was unanimous, in that all specimens fell into monophyletic groups with specimens of known identity.

## Morphological description of live specimens

_Physalia_ specimens are often encountered on the beach after washing ashore, where their anatomy may be compromised by physical damage or decomposition, depending on stranding conditions. We sought to describe these animals from live specimens to better understand differences in the natural morphology and posture of _Physalia_ species as they appear floating in water. We collected and photographed _P. megalista_ and _P. minuta_ specimens from the North Island, New Zealand (May 2024), _P. physalis_ from Gran Canaria, Canary Islands (March 2025), and _P. utriculus_ from the Big Island, Hawai'i (April 2025) and observed macromorphological differences in colony-level features. We supplemented these observations with examination of fixed specimens and designated type material for three species: a lectotype for _P. physalis_, selected from surviving Linnaean syntype material, and neotypes for _P. utriculus_ and _P. megalista_, for which no type material is known to survive. Additionally, to advance our understanding of _P. utriculus_ and _P. mikazuki_ in the Eastern Indian Ocean, we observed and photographed specimens from East Pangandaran Beach, southern coast of West Java, Indonesia (August 2024).

## Usage of generative AI

Generative AI was used in building the ML model described in subsection Image classification via semisupervised learning, and in analysis and manuscript preparation. Under GAIDeT taxonomy [@suchikova2026gaidet], AI was used under human supervision for code generation and creation of algorithms for data analysis from the Software Development and Automation category; data analysis, validation, visualization, and data curation and organization from Data Management; text generation, proofreading and editing, and reformatting from Writing and Editing; and quality assessment and identification of limitations from Supervision. The primary AI model used was Claude Code Opus 5. The authors supervised, verified, and corrected all work done by the model, and take full responsibility for the results presented here.

# Data availability

Mitochondrial genomes are deposited in GenBank under accessions **PZ224317–PZ224484** (n=168). Nuclear 18S sequences are deposited under **PZ802573–PZ802753** (n=181). Nuclear ITS sequences are deposited under accessions **PZ804143–PZ804328** (n=186).

Mitochondrial genomes were assembled for the whole-genome-sequenced Illumina samples only. The 2025 open-ocean samples were sequenced with Oxford Nanopore, and neither their mitochondrial genome assemblies nor the mitochondrial gene markers recovered from them met the quality threshold for deposition; no mitochondrial sequence from those samples is deposited. Those samples are represented in GenBank by their nuclear 18S and ITS sequences, and their species identifications derive from the mitochondrial genome tree provided in the repository below as alignments and treefiles.

Whole-genome sequencing data for the 48 specimens generated in this study (28 ONT, 20 Illumina) are deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject **PRJNA1509992** (SRA study **SRP725477**), comprising Illumina and Oxford Nanopore runs **SRR40085724–SRR40085779** (n=56 runs, including 8 specimens each sequenced across two Illumina flow cells) and BioSample accessions **SAMN62283094–SAMN62283141** (n=48). Per-specimen run accessions are given in S2 Table (`Supp_Table_specimens.tsv`).

All alignments, tree files, analysis code, and the labeled image dataset are available at <https://github.com/shchurch/Physalia_spatiotemporal_patterns>, archived at <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22240661>.

# Supporting Information

**S1 Fig. Effort-corrected seasonal abundance for _Physalia utriculus/mikazuki_ in southern Africa.** Counts of _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ observations by day of year, in the region bounded by 5-45° E and 0-40° S. From top: the baseline of abundant beach species (hermit crabs and echinoderms) used as a proxy for observer activity; unweighted _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ counts; and the same counts corrected for observer effort on a daily and on a seasonal basis. The anomalous peak in late April appears in both the baseline and the unweighted counts, and corresponds to a period of local public holidays rather than to a peak in abundance. It is removed by either correction, after which the underlying seasonal trend is clearer.

**S2 Fig. Seasonal timing of observations, unweighted.** As in the seasonal wheels of Fig 2 and Fig 3 of the main text, but with each observation counted once rather than weighted by observer effort. All four regions are shown together here, so panel letters differ from the main-text figures: (A) the Caribbean and North America, (B) South America, (C) southern Africa, (D) Eastern Australia and New Zealand.

**S3 Fig. Seasonal timing of observations, weighted by daily observer effort.** As in the seasonal wheels of Fig 2 and Fig 3 of the main text, but each observation is divided by the number of baseline beach-species records on that same calendar day, rather than by a cyclic model fitted across the year. Panel order as in S2 Fig. This follows day-to-day activity more closely but is far noisier: in southern Africa and the southwest Atlantic some days carry a single baseline record, so one observation on such a day can weigh a hundred times one on a well-covered day.

**S4 Fig. Seasonal patterns in the southwest Pacific and the western South Atlantic.** Tiles indicate the circular median day for species observations in that area, colored by the calendar wheel at lower right. Grey hexagons hold fewer than three observations, too few to calculate a median. (C,D) South America, for _P. physalis_ (C) and _P. utriculus/mikazuki_ (D). These panels are the counterpart to the main-text seasonal gradients figure, which shows the Caribbean and North America, and southern Africa.

**S5 Fig. Mitochondrial genome tree of all 199 sequenced _Physalia_ samples.** Closely related clades of a single species are collapsed to one tip, giving the number of genomes and the localities they span; other tips give specimen and locality. **S1 Text. Key to the mature colonies of _Physalia_.** Applies to colonies bearing multiple zooids, including visible gonodendra in the main zone.

**1a.** Gastrozooids with a bright yellow distal tip; float glassy and transparent except at the anterior apex (green, yellow or blue) and crest ... 2

**1b.** Gastrozooid tips not yellow (dark blue, blue-green, reddish, or pale cream); float pigmented, opalescent, or colourless but not conspicuously glassy ... 3

**2a.** Main zone with a centrally located principal palpon and tentacle, adjacent palpons and tentacles much smaller; all clusters borne on one cluster base ... _P. utriculus_ (common bluebottle)

**2b.** Main zone with several clusters borne on distinct cluster bases, bearing more than one major tentacle and associated prominent palpon ... provisionally _P. mikazuki_ (crescent helmet bluebottle; see the _Physalia mikazuki_ section in the main text for the caveats on this diagnosis)

**3a.** Clusters borne on several independent cluster bases spaced along the anterior–posterior axis of the float (up to seven clusters in large colonies); crest running nearly the length of the float and capable of being raised to about the height of the float; main and posterior zones usually continuous, without a visible gap; float shaded blue, pink or purple ... _P. physalis_ (Portuguese man-o-war)

**3b.** Clusters borne primarily on a single cluster base (large colonies of _P. megalista_ occasionally with multiple clusters, but central cluster much larger); crest shorter; a distinct gap usually present between the main and posterior zones ... 4

**4a.** Float projecting anteriorly well beyond the anterior insertion of the crest (crest "incomplete"), this projection often held perpendicular to the water surface in disturbed or beached specimens; crest crimped along its dorsal edge; float opalescent purple and blue-green, rarely glassy ... _P. megalista_ (southern bluebottle)

**4b.** Float not projecting beyond the crest insertion; crest smooth dorsally; float colourless apart from a green anterior apex, elongate-cylindrical in fixed material ... 5

**5a.** Main zone bearing several palpons and tentacles of similar maturity, giving a "bunched" appearance; large gonodendra present on a colony of relatively small overall size ... _P. minuta_ (little bluebottle)

**5b.** Main zone with a strong anterior–posterior maturity gradient about the largest palpon ... _P. megalista_ (southern bluebottle), small or relaxed specimen; cf. 4a
